**Wednesday, February 20, 1952**

The United States was at war. Not a cold war — a hot one, fought in the mountains of Korea, where American forces had been engaged since June 1950. That February, the fighting had locked into a stalemate near the 38th parallel, trench warfare not unlike the previous century's Western Front, while armistice negotiations dragged on at Panmunjom. Boys were dying in Korea the week you were born. The world this child entered was a world already at war, already nuclear — and, as it would turn out, nine months away from becoming something more dangerous still.

On November 1, 1952 — when you were eight months old — the United States detonated Ivy Mike at Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific: the first thermonuclear device ever tested. Hundreds of times more powerful than the bomb that had destroyed Hiroshima, it vaporized an entire island. The atomic age became the hydrogen bomb age in the year of your birth. You were born into the last months of the merely atomic world.

Two weeks before you arrived, on February 6, King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham. A twenty-five-year-old Princess Elizabeth became Queen while on safari in Kenya, before she had landed back in Britain. She would reign until September 2022. The world you were born into was fourteen days into a reign you would outlive by only four years. Your childhood, your working life, your middle age, and your early seventies all occurred inside the Elizabethan era — and then it ended, and you were still here.

The Oslo Winter Olympics were underway as you entered the world — the first Winter Games ever held in Scandinavia, running from February 14 to February 25. Norwegian skiers dominated the cross-country events on home snow. It was also the year the Soviet Union first competed in the Summer Olympics, at Helsinki — the Cold War's two great antagonists formally sharing a field of competition for the first time, even as they pointed nuclear weapons at each other's cities.

Now here are two exact-date connections, both of which land directly on your birthday.

**February 20, 1962** — your tenth birthday — John Glenn climbed into a capsule called Friendship 7, perched atop an Atlas rocket, and became the first American to orbit Earth. He circled the planet three times in under five hours. The space race had been going badly; this was the moment the country exhaled. You were ten years old on the day the United States finally caught up to the sky.

**February 20, 1986** — your thirty-fourth birthday — the Soviet Union launched Mir, the space station that would orbit for fifteen years and eventually host astronauts from a dozen countries. From Glenn's solitary capsule on your tenth birthday to the first true long-duration space station on your thirty-fourth: your birthdate has been, more than once, the date the species chose for reaching beyond.

Step back and hold the full distance. You were born before Sputnik (1957), before the first human in space (1961), before the Moon landing (1969). In February 1952 there was no polio vaccine — it wouldn't come until 1955, and children were still being paralyzed in the summers before then. There was no Civil Rights Act. Most American families did not yet own a television. Rock and roll did not exist as a cultural force. Commercial jet travel hadn't begun.

In seventy-four years: the Korean War's inconclusive end; the full arc of the Cold War; the Civil Rights movement; a man on the Moon; Nixon's fall; the personal computer; the AIDS crisis; the Berlin Wall; the Soviet Union's collapse; the internet remaking every dimension of daily life; 9/11; a global pandemic; and now an AI revolution that is changing what it means to know and to think.

The child born that February entered a world at active war, on the edge of the thermonuclear threshold, with a brand-new queen and the first Scandinavian Winter Olympics still underway. All of that felt contemporary then — the stakes felt immediate and the future felt genuinely uncertain. Seventy-four years later, those events are history, the queen is gone, and the world has remade itself so thoroughly that the February 1952 child and the September 2026 world barely seem to belong to the same story.

They do, of course. And you are the connective tissue between them.
